title: Overtime & Crunching in Game Development (vs others)
summary: Game developer shares a small informal survey on overtime, argues most developers work normal hours, and calls crunch a symptom of bad planning rather than a necessity.

assertions.quote: overall in general people work pretty damned normal times

verdicts.note: Industry surveys such as IGDA's find crunch still common in games with roughly half of respondents reporting it, so the picture is mixed; the video's own survey is small and self-selected.

assertions.quote: I think it's a terrible sign of just mismanagement and bad planning

verdicts.note: Postmortems and case studies link crunch to scope and schedule failures, but publisher deadlines, funding and studio culture also drive it, so planning is one cause among several.

assertions.quote: basically driving down their productivity in my opinion and driving down employee happiness

verdicts.note: Labour economics and reviews of overtime research show output per hour falls and errors rise after sustained weeks beyond roughly fifty hours, and burnout studies link crunch to attrition.

The report cites recovery research that feeling overworked blocks detachment from work, which leads to burnout and lower life satisfaction; it does not itself measure crunch or its effect on productivity.

122 weekly observations on WWI munitions workers: output is proportional to hours below 49 h/week, rises at a decreasing rate above it and peaks near 63 h, so output per hour falls once weeks run long; happiness was not measured and the workers were not programmers.

assertions.quote: it's developers who just really love their product and they can't stop working on it

verdicts.note: Surveys find both self-driven and management-driven crunch, and normative pressure makes voluntary overtime hard to separate from expected overtime.

assertions.quote: don't want to get estimates that are out that long they're just inaccurate they're not very useful

verdicts.note: Estimation research consistently finds large optimism bias and variance that grows with horizon, though structured estimation methods narrow the error.

Review of time-prediction studies finds average error of 20-30% and no general bias, but software projects of at least 100 work hours show a median overrun of about 20%, so large-scope estimates are biased low rather than useless.

assertions.quote: the smaller companies tended to have a little bit more overtime

verdicts.note: Based on a small informal survey; broader data on company size and hours in software is inconsistent.

assertions.quote: giving that feel and fun on paper and planned out is a whole lot harder

verdicts.note: A judgment about the nature of the work rather than a measurable claim.
